scene.testo: In just 12 minutes, you go from sitting on the ground to floating in orbit. The ride takes you to 17,500 mph. And the part that scares engineers most is not the launch. It is the fiery trip home.
So what is it really like inside the SpaceX Dragon capsule? Where do you sit? Where do you sleep, eat, and use the toilet? And what happens when the screens go silent during reentry?
Stay with me. Because the most dangerous moment is not the launch. It is a seven minute blackout on the way home, when nobody on Earth can talk to you at all.

Meet the ship. Dragon first flew in 2010 as a cargo vessel for the International Space Station. It completed 23 cargo missions over ten years, and that record gave NASA the confidence to trust it with people.
The crew version flew its first test in 2019. Then on May 30, 2020, it became the first American spacecraft to carry astronauts to orbit since the Space Shuttle retired in 2011.
Now imagine standing next to it. The capsule itself is about 16 feet tall and 13 feet wide. Under it sits the trunk, adding roughly 12 more feet. Together, that is taller than a two story house.

The trunk is not just storage. It carries unpressurized cargo, and it supports the spacecraft's power system. It also has fins, which only matter if something goes wrong and Dragon must fly through air alone.
On the nose sits a hinged cover. When it opens, it reveals a docking port for trips to the space station. On some missions, a glass dome window sits there instead, for pure sightseeing.
Dragon has two kinds of thrusters. Sixteen small Draco engines steer the capsule and adjust its orbit. They burn two fuels that ignite on contact, so there is no spark needed, only a valve opening.
The other engines are the SuperDracos. Eight of them sit in four pods around the capsule. Each one can push with about 16,000 pounds of thrust. They exist for one reason only: to save your life.
If the rocket fails during ascent, those engines fire in about a tenth of a second. They throw the capsule away from the booster, covering roughly half a mile in just seven seconds.
Inside, the cabin offers about 330 cubic feet of pressurized space. That sounds tiny. But for a spacecraft, it is roomy. It is about the size of the inside of a large van.
Look forward and you will not find a wall of switches. Apollo capsules had panels packed with dials and toggles. Dragon has three big touchscreens, and that is basically it. The ship flies itself.

If something needs a manual fix, ground teams can often handle it remotely. The astronauts mostly monitor and watch. They are passengers with a very good view, and a very important job in emergencies.
Before anyone climbs in, they put on the suit. Each astronaut gets a custom fitted pressure suit and a helmet made with 3D printing. It is slim, flexible, and designed to be worn the whole ride.

Why bother? Because the suit is the backup plan. If the cabin ever lost pressure, the suit keeps breathable air around you. Without pressure, bodily fluids can literally begin to boil at the temperatures of space.
Launch day starts about three hours before liftoff. The crew suits up at Kennedy Space Center in Florida, gets a final briefing, and then walks out toward a row of waiting Tesla vehicles.
They ride to the launch pad. About an hour before liftoff, an elevator lifts them 255 feet to the crew access arm. That is roughly the height of a 25 story building, with the rocket beside you.
At the top, you cross a short walkway into the capsule. Ground crews help you slide through the side hatch, strap you in, and clip your boots to the floor, so your legs stay put during launch.
Then a hose connects to your suit. It pumps in cooled air, keeping your temperature and breathing comfortable. From this moment on, you and the spacecraft are basically one connected system.
About 45 minutes before liftoff, the ground crew says goodbye and closes the hatch. The access arm swings away. Helmet visors come down. Now it is just you, your crewmates, and the countdown.

Next comes an unusual detail. Fueling begins with the crew already aboard. Most rockets fuel before people board. But SpaceX loads super cold propellant while astronauts sit on top, and they can hear it flowing.
Then the final seconds. Nine Merlin engines ignite at the base of the Falcon 9 booster. Together they produce about 1.8 million pounds of thrust. The whole stack shakes, and then it rises.

Within about a minute, the rocket passes the speed of sound. Pressure builds and the ride gets rough. You feel yourself pushed back into the seat, harder and harder, as the rocket gets lighter and faster.

At about two minutes and thirty seconds, the first stage shuts down and separates. You are already traveling thousands of miles per hour, more than 50 miles up. The upper stage ignites to finish the job.
At roughly nine minutes, the engine cuts off. You are now moving around 17,500 mph, about 125 miles up. The shaking stops. Everything goes quiet. And a stuffed toy floats up in front of you.
scene.q: zero gravity indicator floating plush Dragon

scene.testo: That floating toy is a tradition. It is the signal that you have reached weightlessness. It is a simple, almost silly, detail. But everyone on board knows exactly what it means. You made it.

Around twelve minutes after liftoff, Dragon separates from the second stage. About fifteen minutes in, you lift your visor, unbuckle, and float free. The most dangerous part of going up is behind you.
Now there are two kinds of trips. If you are headed to the International Space Station, the chase takes about a day. Dragon slowly closes the gap, then docks on its own, with astronauts watching.
The other kind of trip is a free flyer mission. Private crews, like Inspiration4 in September 2021, spent about three days in orbit. No station. Just the capsule, the view, and the planet below.
On those flights, the docking port gets replaced by a glass dome. You can put your head inside it and see the horizon in almost every direction. Many people say it is the best seat in the sky.

Now the question everyone asks. Where do you go to the bathroom? Early astronauts had it rough. On Mercury, the first American in space, Alan Shepard, had to wait on the pad so long that he relieved himself in his suit.
Later missions used collection bags, and the Space Shuttle introduced a vacuum toilet. The station uses one too. Air flow, not gravity, pulls everything away. It is not glamorous, but it works.
Dragon has its own toilet, tucked into the wall above the side hatch. It uses fans, valves, and suction hoses. There is even a privacy curtain. In a cabin this small, that curtain matters a lot.

And you cannot really hold it. Astronauts have reported that weightlessness changes how the body behaves, so everyone ends up using the toilet within hours of arriving in orbit. Nobody gets to be shy.
Eating is simpler. Meals come as packaged food that is heated with water or warmed in a small device. Drinks come in pouches with straws, because a loose liquid ball is a mess waiting to happen.
Sleeping is just as strange. There is no up or down, so you float. On long flights, crews use sleeping bags tied to a wall. On short trips, you might just drift and rest in your seat.

Then comes the trip home. Mission control picks one of seven landing zones off Florida, in the Gulf of Mexico or the Atlantic. Weather decides everything. If the seas are rough, the whole plan can wait.
Dragon lowers its orbit step by step, until it is on a path that must hit the atmosphere. Crew suit up again, visors down, straps tight. This is the point of no return, and everyone knows it.
Then the trunk is dropped. The Draco thrusters turn the heat shield toward Earth. From here on, the capsule is on its own. There is no engine to save you. Only the shield, and physics.
Dragon hits the air at about 17,500 mph. The air in front of it compresses so hard that it glows as superheated plasma, around 3,500 degrees Fahrenheit. Outside your window, the world turns orange.

And now the blackout. The plasma blocks radio signals, so for about seven minutes the capsule is cut off. If something goes wrong, nobody tells you. The heat shield tiles slowly burn away, carrying the heat off.

Inside, you stay surprisingly cool. The life support system keeps pumping chilled air through your suit. But the deceleration is brutal. You feel four to five times your normal weight, pressing into your seat.
When the fire fades, radio comes back. Two small drogue parachutes open first, then four huge main parachutes. They slow the capsule to about 15 mph, just fast enough to splash down safely.
After splashdown, a recovery ship rushes in. Crews hoist the capsule onto the deck. Its bright white paint is now scorched into shades of gray and black. But you are safe, and you are back.
One more surprise. Before anyone opens the hatch, teams must cover the thruster nozzles. The fuel is toxic, and they wear breathing masks. Only when the air is safe do they let the crew out.
scene.q: recovery team Dragon hatch open astronauts

scene.testo: After weeks in weightlessness, your legs may feel like jelly. Some astronauts walk with help. And that is life inside Dragon: a few minutes of fire, days of floating, and a view nobody forgets.

descrizione:
What really happens to astronauts inside the SpaceX Dragon capsule? From launch to splashdown, this is life inside Crew Dragon: how astronauts eat, sleep, use the space toilet, and survive a seven minute reentry blackout.

We follow a real mission step by step: the ride to orbit at 17,500 mph, floating in weightlessness, docking at the space station, and returning to Earth through 3,500°F plasma, all explained with documented NASA facts.
